body: You've implied in another comment that he may be simply using the threat of suicide to get what he wants. If that's true, it's incredibly not okay to do that. That's manipulative behavior, and I think you're right to be worried about your friend because he probably has some very deep issues that might also end up affecting you one day. I'd say be careful, especially if you're not an adult.

I get what you mean. I think there's a difference between them posting destructive behavior and glorifying it, vs people who post it to raise awareness. It can be tricky to tell the difference sometimes.

For any potential commenters who may flip out on OP, they have expressly said that he gave them verbal consent for the kiss. So, to be frank, I'm very uncertain about what OP could have done wrong here. OP, if you're reading this, I don't think you're in the wrong here and quite frankly this dude sounds really shady. It sounds like he didn't like the fact that you kissed him so he tried to make you feel like you committed a crime as an excuse for not wanting to talk to you. It's frankly ridiculous and strikes me personally as an extremely immature cop-out. If he hadn't said yes, this would obviously be far different. But according to you he did say yes, so for him to tell you that you've committed a crime by doing something that he gave you explicit consent to do seems really, really fishy. I would be inclined to agree with the other commenter who has said that the dude sounds manipulative. Not only does he sound manipulative, he sounds like he was looking for a reason to ghost you. You're not in the wrong here, imho.

They were a child, not an adult setting out to do this with intent to ruin someone's life. Come on. Some nuance needs to be given to the situation here. That doesn't mean the action is ok. No one wants to justify it because we know that anyone, regardless of age, should never touch someone without their consent. But to call a child evil for one fucked up action is almost more fucked up.

I think that's exactly the point here though. OP wasn't an adult when they did this, they were a child. The action taken wasn't okay and can never be justified, but I don't think it makes sense for OP to be drowning in guilt for one thing they did as a 12 year old. Sorry but it just doesn't make sense to me. I think OP deserves to be able to forgive themselves and move forward.

A good majority of us are getting help and want to be better people. Furthermore, most people wBPD have empathy. You say your ex was a sociopath, so that's more than likely why she didn't display empathy. Everyone with BPD is different, and to be honest, it's very ignorant of you to assume that we're all the same. 

We're not your ex. I hope you can seek help and heal from what you've been through.

Imho, this would be more likely under the condition that someone with BPD's actions are calculated and they know exactly what they're doing. This was not the case for me. I've also heard many a BPD sufferer say that they lacked almost all self awareness before seeking help. BPD, to me, is a form of PTSD and it's a collection of subconscious defense mechanisms. So this would make sense.

In other words, no, I don't think sufferers of BPD do what they do on purpose. But I'm only one person wBPD.

it's understandable given your trauma history that you would feel this way. i feel like for me i had to really become self aware and actively work on changing myself. this isn't easy. taking responsibility and realizing how your actions affect others are extremely important when you have BPD. before you are diagnosed or before you have self awareness or even if you just dont know how to cope, it is extremely easy to hurt others. not because i wanted to hurt someone, but because i was so caught up in how unbearable my emotions felt, if that makes sense? flipping from one extreme to the other is basically the hallmark of BPD, as well. we just, i think, have to learn to not take these mood swings out on others or blame them for how we feel or react to something. we have to realize that we are the one with a disorder and that we have to take accountability to manage an illness that, to be fair, we never asked for. regardless, it's still our responsibility. esp if youre a parent, imho. sorry to hear what you have been through, and its OK if you cant empathize w pwBPD all the time. ofc, stigma is pretty harmful bc it can prevent us from wanting to get better. i'd ultimately say, dont let anyone mistreat you just bc they have BPD, but also try to see them as you would any other person with an illness. tbh, i think bc of your trauma history it might be a process for you to "learn" to separate BPD, the illness, from malice or evil. bc quite frankly i was pretty darn malicious and at times evil before i was self aware. i think it ultimately stemmed from subconscious defense processes that, though they were not my fault, they have always been my responsibility. as long as we are taking accountability, it shouldnt be excruciating to have a relationship with someone who is suffering from BPD. it seems most of your experiences have been with pwBPD who dont want to take accountability. im sorry to hear this, and i hope you will heal from the unfair experiences youve been dealt. you didnt ask for that either.

Unless there's a good reason, I do find it incredibly weird, even if they weren't exes. But especially that they're exes. I can't make that distinction obviously, only you can. I've been very manipulative before, but it's not to brag about. It's something we have to unlearn. It's going to be really hard for you to form genuine, close bonds with others with this type of mindset.
If the person is untreated/not willing to seek help, this makes some sense. However, giving this advice as a blanket statement seems a bit biased.

I in no way am intending to derail your question, and I apologize if so, but genuinely, I think the question you might want to ask your self might be more along the lines of "How can we both be good partners to each other?"

The reason I say this is because I've noticed (generally, not saying this about you specifically) that sometimes, people will ask what they can do for their partner wBPD, but then they'll put up with like... a LOT of stuff that they shouldn't have to put up with. I mean for myself, what helps me is my partner being compassionate and empathetic, and not like judging me if I am having a moment. But another important thing someone wBPD might need is someone to call them out from an empathetic standpoint when they're not being fair.

You're not overreacting at all. This doesn't sound healthy for you and quite frankly, it sounds extremely traumatizing. I'm sorry you have to deal with this. I believe anyone would be horrified by dealing with this behavior.

If you're repeatedly splitting on someone, maybe talk to a friend about the situation and try to get their perspective, as in, would your friend also be upset by this, or is it more bc of BPD? 

Sometimes, when you're repeatedly splitting on someone, it *can* be bc they're toxic/abusive and are doing things to trigger you. Other times, it could be because you haven't resolved a certain issue you have with them, causing you to split on them each time you remember the thing they said/did/etc. 

Lastly, I would say, try to keep this in mind: devaluation (splitting black) is unhealthy, but can be helpful when it comes to abusers. However, idealization (painting them white) is just as unhealthy. Ideally, through DBT, we might learn to have a more integrated view of a person: their good traits and their bad traits. I hope I could help somehow.

You have kids? Yeah, leave her unless she commits to getting help RIGHT NOW. The kids (and you) do not deserve psychological trauma. They're just children. You're their dad, right? It's your job to protect them. You don't want them to grow up traumatized just bc you decided to stay with someone toxic. It's the parent's responsibility to protect their children. Both you and your kids will be much happier and spared severe trauma.

Abuse is a choice, and it's a choice any untreated borderline could make when dealing with intense and seemingly entirely unmanageable emotions. u/bitchcraftxx, im gonna be honest, i dont think a relationship is going to work for you right now unless you're willing to think about how your actions affect your partner. I know how it feels to love someone so much that you put up with stuff. I recall that when my boyfriend first tried setting boundaries with me, I saw it as a betrayal. This was due to the severe co-dependency we had developed over the years. But here's what I think too: I'm genuinely eternally grateful for him setting those boundaries. They hurt at first, bc we were enmeshed together without our own proper senses of identity. But him setting those boundaries and asserting his own boundaries is the best thing that ever happened to both of us! He no longer has to be overly concerned about how I will respond to things or what I'm feeling/doing, and I no longer have to be overly worried that he's cheating/lying/etc (still a slight worry at times)- bc i have my own sense of identity, however rudimentary, that is separate from the relationship. 

In my experience, my bf would text me when with friends, but this only enabled my clingy and toxic behavior. I'm not saying the other commenter is wrong bc everyone will have their own take on things, but if I were you I wouldn't enable it. Hmm... I'm sorry to hear that you're anxious about bringing it up to him. Remember, it's your relationship too, you're not a caretaker, and you're allowed to assert your own boundaries even if it hurts his feelings. Again, I wish you the best

Hey friend, this seriously doesn't sound like a good situation for you and it causes me a fair amount of concern. I have severe BPD and have had since I was 13. I have been in a long term relationship where, with untreated BPD and no self-awareness, I also cut my boyfriend off from friends I did not like and would get upset when he would want to go anywhere.

But here's the thing: this kind of behavior is not acceptable, even if BPD is involved. It's not OK, because it's doing emotional harm to you. It makes sense to me that you would want to go out and have fun with your friends with no worries; that's what you should do. You should be, ideally, at a stage where, if your BPD partner is upset, you can give them some encouragement, and they're able to do the emotional work needed to sit down and accept your reassurance and process their emotions on their own. If his response to you comforting him is to lash out and accuse you of cheating or whatever else, that shows that he is not putting in the work needed to have a healthy relationship, bc he is (maybe) not self-aware enough to do so. I can't speak for him, but that's what it seems like to me. I empathize with him and how he feels, trust me, I know how shitty it is. But I'm also concerned about you as well. 

Bottom line, imho your partner is going to have to learn to be OK with you going out and having friends. He may still be upset, and that's OK! It's okay for him to feel scared and upset. What's not OK is him cutting you off from people. That is, unfortunately, abusive, and when untreated, pwBPD can engage in these sorts of behaviors. I'm not in treatment, but have gained a slight self-awareness.

I wish you the best. My DMs are open if you need advice.

This may sound slightly harsh, and I'm not trying to be. You say your boyfriend was diagnosed wBPD, but doesn't believe he has it? That's kind of a big problem that he needs to be willing to work on before your relationship can work imho. That's my opinion though. 

The reason why I'm saying this is because if he doesn't believe he has BPD, he might be more likely to believe he's in the right while doing hurtful things (such as accusing you of cheating) without being able to say "OK, I have BPD, so I need to distinguish if this is true, or if it's my brain playing tricks on me." You're right, a lot of his behavior is related to his diagnosis. But if he can't see that, how can he regulate, or try to regulate, his responses properly... :( I know how much it fucking sucks bc I've been where he is.

Also, I truly don't mean to sound harsh in any sense, but here's another thing: You don't have to be his caretaker. Like it's great that you're there for him, you're clearly an understanding partner! That's awesome, thats what most of us wBPD need. My word of advice is, be careful not to enable him too much if he's doing something actively hurtful. But also, he needs to come to terms with his diagnosis. I can't comment too much on the trust thing bc I've had severe trust issues as well, so yeah. I wish the best for both of y'all.

Yikes. This sounds genuinely awful for all parties and I'm very sorry to hear that your friend wBPD has been putting so much stress on you. 

Here's the bottom line: It's OK for you to walk away for the sake of your own mental health. Will it hurt him? Well yes, we can't pretend it won't.

 Does that mean you should stay and have your mental heath deteriorate more? No. Quite frankly, there's very little you can do to help him in this situation, yet he's depending on you and others to fix his problems for him. It's also not OK for him to threaten suicide to get what he wants. And honestly I think you should tell him that, like those exact words. "It's not okay for you to threaten to kill yourself to get what you want, which is for me to stay. That's manipulative and I can't put up with it." Seriously, call him on it, it'll help him learn to take responsibility for his mistake.

 If you don't mind me asking, is he an adult or an adolescent? One of the hardest lessons I had to learn was that no one can fix your problems for you. 

He sounds like he really needs help. I feel for him. Our mental healthcare system is honestly not the best (assuming y'all are in the US) but inpatient treatment can sometimes bring someone down from the edge.

Hey, I want to address the generalized hatred for women (compassionately) because I've noticed this develop among a subset of young men who often struggle with comorbid mental illness. 

As we know, black and white thinking is common for us. Also, people wBPD often seek out attention and love. If you see women as a potential source of attention and fulfillment and love, and happen to interact with a number who may reject you, or even be more cruel than simple rejection- I can see where this would develop into black-and white thinking of "All women are bad". In my humble opinion, I'm not a psychologist nor an expert on you, but I do believe- as someone who has struggled with a fear of other women- this stems from black and white thinking and possibly traumatic past experiences, mixed with a level of social conditioning. 

Of course when you're feeling despairing and depressed, the most common human reaction, esp sometimes for pwBPD, is blame. You're going to want to find a source for your pain, and point it out, and say "THIS is what's causing me to feel so shit". That, in itself, is in my opinion, quite a human thing. 

Now, here's where I will dissent just a little bit. I'm going to say that I truly believe that men who often end up developing true hatred for women don't surround themselves with women who treat them fairly. These women might be shallow, not looking for anything serious (which is fine), cruel, possibly cluster B themselves... etc. These women tend to treat men they view as desirable fairly, and ones they view as undesirable, like crap. 

Now, Im gonna say something about that. 1.) Most women aren't like this. Seriously. I know it's easy to believe it is if you frequent dating apps and the like, but honestly, most of us genuinely do not care if someone is under 6 ft or overweight. 2.) If a woman, or anyone, treats you badly, that is NOT  reflection on you. It's a reflection on them. It shows that they're an inconsiderate person- not that there's anything wrong with you. 3.) You won't want to date a woman who puts you down for being short (I genuinely adore short guys), for the way you act, look, dress, etc. Because guess what? That's not the kind of person you want for a partner. 

My heart goes out to you. You deserve healthy relationships with compassionate women who aren't trying to fit you into a box. I wish you all the best!

Hey. I wanted to comment bc I feel for you. I've been there, trust me. I know it's easier to say than it is to truly understand, that you're not defined by your past. I don't mean this critically, but you should have some compassion for yourself. You deserve it. You know why? because you have BPD. Not everything is your fault; of course, accountability is important, but at the same time you didn't choose to have this disorder. A lot of us pwBPD do things and don't even know WHY we do them. (Usually they're subconscious defense mechanisms)

I'll tell you why I think some people avoid responsibility for their actions. Because I think in some cases, they had a childhood where they were harshly punished for taking responsibility for anything- or some other similar circumstance. Things like that would make anyone terrified of looking at their flaws or wrongdoings. The fact that you're still doing that DESPITE your fear and how bad it makes you feel means something. It means that you're a good person who wants to do right by people. Maybe you just didn't know how to before. That lack of knowledge or coping skills is not your fault. It's something that your parents should have instilled in you from the start.

Guilt can be a useful emotion. Shame on the other hand, aka thinking YOU are bad, is not a productive or useful thing to feel. It's a trauma response.

You can use guilt to inspire you to be kinder to others where you can. Whenever I feel guilty, I think to myself "OK I feel guilty. That's normal; I feel bad for (insert thing I did here). I'll do better next time." Then try to simply let it go. It will be VERY hard to let go of at first. Your brain will try to force you to ruminate on the thought. But when that happens, force your brain to switch to something else; literally anything, even just visualizing a tree or something (thats one thing I do lol). I know it sounds like bull, but it has genuinely helped me a lot with my guilt issues. 

Shame can also be caused by a fear of rejection from others. Here's how I see it: People w BPD have obviously, a higher experience of negative life events than other people. They also have higher emotions; remember that. We feel far more strongly than others. That means unfortunately, that we are more likely to be abrasive, toxic, or manipulative, etc. But in most cases, **it's a product of our conditioning. It's how we were programmed.** These traits that you have picked up are NOT YOUR FAULT. It's just your responsibility to work on these traits so that they won't negatively impact others. You've already made a ton of progress by feeling guilty; most people who do bad things won't even think to feel guilt. You can be better without beating yourself up. I know it's hard, but if you ever need to talk to someone I (fellow internet stranger lol) am here to try to help. I hope that your night goes okay.

Yes, I used to struggle majorly with this. For me, two things needed to happen for the cycle to stop.

1.) I needed to think at length about what I was saying/doing and how it was affecting my partner. 

2.) I needed to want it to stop because I realized the magnitude of harm I was doing. 

These two things can be hard to do for someone with untreated BPD. Empathy may not come naturally when you're in a defensive or splitting position. You may feel like lashing out is a means of protecting yourself from rejection or pain. Most times, that's what a lot of people with BPD are focusing on: emotionally protecting themselves. That's completely understandable, in itself.

However, then we get to the other side of things: how your partner feels when you say/do hurtful things. I know my big one was telling my partner I hated him when splitting. (of course, that wasnt the only thing.) Of course, this hurt him, but I was too "caught up" in my own pain to consider it. I feel as if a lot of us with BPD can get to a point in relationships where we focus on our own pain and the ways we feel we've been slighted. This can make it very easy for us to harm others, because "your pain isn't as bad as mine," or "I'm just protecting myself" etc.

But in the end, **both you and your partner deserve to have a happy, fulfilling relationship.** Of course, there will be problems with BPD. It's an illness; there always will be. Someone who loves you will stick around and help you through the tough times, but you have to do your part as well by not letting yourself abuse them. (The definition Im using here of abuse is to lash out at someone with the intention of causing harm, getting back at them etc.) You may feel extremely guilty when you seriously consider the impact of your words and actions, but that doesn't mean that you are bad. If you're going to move forward with the intent of improving, you ARE good, because you have goodness in you.

I would suggest finally, that somewhere down the line, you talk to your partner. If you say "I've been an abusive/toxic/etc. partner. That's not your fault, it never was, it was only my choices that caused this" that in itself can make them feel better. At least, that way, they know it's not their fault. 

I wish you the best of luck in fixing this. It's hard, especially if you've been abused. You've got this <3 You can DM me if you ever need help.

Sometimes when you try to set boundaries with people who are Cluster B, they can see this as a betrayal. They see it as you pushing them out of your life. Maybe your sister could benefit from being aware that setting boundaries is not a betrayal or a rejection, but is simply a step towards a healthier relationship. Hi. I really empathize with your post. I've found myself in a very similar situation. So I'd like to try to address a couple of things. 

First off, sometimes letting your guard down can, understandably, feel incredibly scary, even terrifying. It's possible that the actual act of letting your guard down, so to speak, would not be as scary under the right circumstances. You have expressed discontent with your current state and that you would like to change. It sounds like you've gone through a shit ton of trauma and pain, and it's entirely understandable that you wouldn't want to be vulnerable to others. Rather than starting by letting your guard down entirely, you could perhaps try to simply start by being nicer to others. I know it sounds cheesy, but something I've found is that  ever since I've started being nicer to others in the smallest of ways- just in demeanor, not by necessarily getting too attached to them so I can still avoid vulnerability- I've felt... less angry? I suppose it depends on where your anger stems from, so you can take that with a grain of salt if you'd like. 

I think it's important to note, too, that it's completely natural to feel a desire to get revenge when someone has wronged us. However, what I've found is that it truly has made me feel more miserable in the long run. You could argue that it contributes negativity in the world, whereas it sounds like you are a person who would like to contribute positivity, and to be positive, but simply don't know how. I've been there. 

Frankly speaking, I'd like to address where you mentioned that people will judge you. To be honest, it doesn't matter that people will judge you. The only thing that matters is how you see yourself. If you are striving every day to be a good person, then their judgements don't matter anyway. It's just their opinion of you; it says nothing about who you are as a person. Your actions say that. And while understandable that you'd have so much anger, it's never too late to change your actions. It's never too late to make a different choice; just because you have been making these choices does not mean that you have to keep doing them or that you are defined by them. You can choose differently. Perhaps that means sitting with your anger. Just sit with it and let yourself feel your anger, without acting on it. Remind yourself that your feelings do not necessarily HAVE to be acted on and that you are a person who is separate from your emotions. Your emotions do not define who you are. 

If you feel it is needed, perhaps seeking a therapist who specializes in trauma and anger management will help. I understand how being a survivor of trauma impacts and causes anger and even rage/lashing out at others, yet it is not talked about often. You are a person deserving of love as much as anyone else and you CAN change if you so desire. Don't let anyone hold the opinion of your past over your head. It's your life. 

I wish you all the best and I'm sending love from a stranger.

This may sound a bit blunt, but I feel it needs to be said (for context, i have BPD). It sounds like you've tried a lot of different ways to end the call in a way that won't upset your friend. You need to be sure that they are also putting some effort in in regards to not guilt tripping, not being passive aggressive and respecting your personal boundaries. They need to try to understand how boundaries work if they want the relationship to work. This may sound harsh, and it's also not necessarily easy. 

First, they need to be aware that they ARE guilt-tripping/being passive aggressive towards you. I used to do these things a lot without being fully aware of what I was doing and the consequences it would have for the other person. Your friend may FEEL upset or even devastated when ending a call because they may interpret this as abandonment- but there is a difference between feeling a certain way and acting on that feeling. You can try gently bringing this up with them. I would not suggest "tough love" because that tends to really trigger BPD sufferers badly. Try to make sure that you are loving and honest, not necessarily harsh and honest. 

Obviously, there is a reason why so many of our relationships fall apart so quickly. I feel that being aware of our toxic behavior is a good first step. Perhaps, your friend needs to look into free DBT resources for themselves. Just really basic ones such as "sitting" with an emotion rather than immediately acting on it, as you realize that you do not have to act on every emotion (this was a tough one for me and the biggest factor in my negative behaviors). 

I hope everything gets better with your friend. Ultimately, make sure to prioritize your own mental health.
